statement:
Let $k$ be a positive integer, and let $G_1,\dots,G_k$ be complete graphs, each
having exactly $k$ vertices, such that $|V(G_i)\cap V(G_j)|\le 1$ for all $i\neq
j$. Let $G$ be their union, i.e. the graph with vertex set
$V(G)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}V(G_i)$ and edge set $E(G)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}E(G_i)$. Then
$G$ admits a proper colouring with $k$ colours: there exists a map
$c\colon V(G)\to\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(u)\neq c(v)$ for every edge
$uv\in E(G)$; equivalently, $\chi(G)\le k$.

Equivalently, in hypergraph language: let $H$ be an $n$-uniform linear
hypergraph with exactly
$n$ hyperedges, that is, a hypergraph in which every hyperedge contains exactly $n$
vertices and any two distinct hyperedges share at most one vertex. Then there is
a colouring of the vertices of $H$ with $n$ colours such that every hyperedge
contains exactly one vertex of each colour.

For a finite simple graph $G$ and a set $S \subseteq V(G)$, let $c(G -
S)$ denote the number of connected components of the graph obtained from $G$ by
deleting $S$. For a real number $t \ge 0$, call $G$
$t$-tough if for every integer $k > 1$ and every $S \subseteq V(G)$ with $c(G -
S) \ge k$ one has $|S| \ge tk$; equivalently, $G$ is $t$-tough if

$$
|S| \ge t \cdot c(G - S) \quad \text{for every } S \subseteq V(G) \text{ with } c(G - S) > 1 .
$$

(Under this convention every complete graph is $t$-tough for every $t$, since
deleting vertices never leaves more than one component.) A graph $G$ on $n \ge
3$ vertices is Hamiltonian if it contains a cycle passing through each of its $n$
vertices exactly once.

There exists a real number $t$ such that every $t$-tough graph on at least $3$
vertices is Hamiltonian.

Let $H$ be a finite undirected graph. For graphs $G$ and $H$, say that $G$ is
$H$-free if no induced subgraph of $G$ is isomorphic to
$H$; that is, there is no subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ such that the graph $G[S]$
obtained by restricting $G$ to $S$ (keeping exactly those edges of
$G$ with both ends in $S$) is isomorphic to $H$. A clique of $G$ is a set of
pairwise adjacent vertices, and an independent set of $G$ is a set of pairwise
non-adjacent vertices.

For every finite undirected graph $H$ there exist constants $\delta_H >
0$ and $c_H > 0$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ on $n \ge
1$ vertices contains a clique of size at least $c_H
n^{\delta_H}$ or an independent set of size at least $c_H n^{\delta_H}$.

Equivalently, for every hereditary class
$\mathcal{F}$ of finite graphs (closed under taking induced subgraphs) that is not the class of all finite graphs, there exists $\delta_{\mathcal{F}}
> 0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph in
$\mathcal{F}$ has a clique or an independent set of size $\Omega\!\left(n^{\delta_{\mathcal{F}}}\right)$.

All graphs below are finite, simple and undirected.

For a graph $G=(V,E)$, a *vertex-deleted subgraph* of $G$ is a subgraph
$G-v$ obtained by deleting exactly one vertex $v \in
V$ together with all edges incident to it; it is an induced subgraph of $G$. The
*deck* of $G$ is the multiset

$$
D(G) = \{\!\{\, [G-v] \;:\; v \in V \,\}\!\},
$$

where $[H]$ denotes the isomorphism class of $H$; the members of
$D(G)$ are called *cards*. Two graphs $G$ and $H$ are *hypomorphic* if $D(G) =
D(H)$ as multisets.

An *edge-deleted subgraph* of $G$ is a subgraph $G-e$ obtained by deleting
exactly one edge $e \in E$ (keeping all vertices), and the *edge-deck* of $G$ is
the multiset

$$
ED(G) = \{\!\{\, [G-e] \;:\; e \in E \,\}\!\}.
$$

**(1) Reconstruction.** For every pair of graphs $G$ and $H$ with
$|V(G)| = |V(H)| \ge 3$, if $D(G) = D(H)$ then $G \cong H$.

**(2) Set reconstruction.** For every pair of graphs $G$ and $H$ with
$|V(G)| = |V(H)| \ge 4$, if the *sets* of isomorphism classes of vertex-deleted
subgraphs of $G$ and of $H$ coincide, that is, if $D(G)$ and $D(H)$ have the
same underlying set, then $G \cong H$.

**(3) Edge reconstruction.** For every pair of graphs $G$ and $H$ with at least
four edges, if $ED(G) = ED(H)$ then $G \cong H$.
Is it true that a clutter has the MFMC property if and only if it has the packing property?
Is it true that every smooth polytope has the integer decomposition property?
Any $2k$-edge-connected (possibly infinite) multigraph admits a $k$-edge-connected orientation.
Let $M$ be a matroid of rank n whose ground set S can be partitioned into n disjoint bases $B_1,\dots,B_n$. Is it true that $B_1,\dots,B_n$ always have n disjoint transversals that are bases of $M$?
Is it true that if D=(V,A) is a digraph where every node has positive out-degree, then D has a quasi-kernel of size at most |V|/2?
Is it true that if the hypergraph $H$ has no isolated vertices and all of its hyperedges are finite, then $H$ admits a strongly minimal edge cover?
For every $r\geq 4$ and $k\geq 2$ is there some finite $f(k,r)$ such that every graph of chromatic number $\geq f(k,r)$ contains a subgraph of girth $\geq r$ and chromatic number $\geq k$?
Let $k\geq 1$. What is the best possible $c_k$ such that $ R(C_{2k+1},H)\leq c_k m $ for any graph $H$ on $m$ edges without isolated vertices?
If $G$ is an $n$-vertex graph in which at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $n/2$, must $G$ contain every tree on at most $n/2$ vertices?

For which graphs $G_1,G_2$ is it true that


-  for every $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $H$ without a $G_1$ but if the edges of $H$ are $n$-coloured then there is a monochromatic copy of $G_2$, and yet

-  for every graph $H$ without a $G_1$ there is an $\aleph_0$-colouring of the edges of $H$ without a monochromatic $G_2$.

The cochromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\zeta(G)$, is the minimum number of colours needed to colour the vertices of $G$ such that each colour class induces either a complete graph or empty graph. The dichromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\delta(G)$, is the minimum number $k$ of colours required such that, in any orientation of the edges of $G$, there is a $k$-colouring of the vertices of $G$ such that there are no monochromatic oriented cycles.
Must a graph with large chromatic number have large dichromatic number? Must a graph with large cochromatic number contain a graph with large dichromatic number?

Let $r\geq 2$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ be such that $A_i
ot\subseteq A_j$ for all $i\neq j$ and for any $t$ if there exists some $i$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$ then there must exist at least $r$ sets of that size.
How large must $n$ be (as a function of $r$) to ensure that there is such a family which achieves $n-3$ distinct sizes of sets?

Let $k\geq 3$ and define $F_k(n)$ to be the minimal $r$ such that there is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ many edges such that the edges can be $r$-coloured so that every subgraph isomorphic to $C_{2k+1}$ has no colour repeating on the edges.
Is it true that $ F_k(n)\sim n^2/8? $
Does there exist a $3$-critical $3$-uniform hypergraph in which every vertex has degree at least $7$?

Let $k\geq 3$ and $A$ be an additive basis of order $k$. Does there exist a constant $c=c(k)>0$ such that if $r(n)\geq c\log n$ for all large $n$ then $A$ must contain a minimal basis of order $k$? (Here $r(n)$ counts the number of representations of $n$ as the sum of at most $k$ elements from $A$.)

A critical vertex, edge, or set of edges, is one whose deletion lowers the chromatic number.
Let $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$. Must there exist a graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ such that every vertex is critical, yet every critical set of edges has size $>r$?
